messages.subject: On the efficiency of the mixed effect model
parts:
Dear stan team,

First of all, thank you very much for the efforts on providing us the excellent software "Stan". I am using Rstan and asking for advise on taking advantage of stan software for a mixed effect model.

I am a new user for "stan" and trying to learn an efficient way to program with stan. The session information is as follows:

My code on the mixed effect model is as follows:

data {
int<lower=0> N_subj;     // usually large = 1000
int<lower=0> N_obs;      // usually smaller = 200
int<lower=0> K_x;         // can be 30
real Y[N_subj];
matrix[N_obs, K_x] E;
matrix[N_subj, N_obs] W;
}

parameters {
real mp;
vector[K_x] beta;
matrix[N_subj, K_x] xi;
real<lower=0> taureg;
real<lower=0> taueps;
real<lower=0> ll[K_x];
}

transformed parameters {
real<lower = 0> sq_taureg;
real<lower = 0> sq_taueps;
        vector[N_subj]  mean_part;
sq_taureg <- 1/sqrt(taureg);
sq_taueps <- 1/sqrt(taueps);
mean_part <- mp + xi * beta;
}

model {

    for (i in 1:N_subj)
xi[i] ~ normal(0, ll);
   
for (i in 1:K_x){
ll[i] ~ inv_gamma(0.01,0.01);
beta[i]  ~ normal(0,100);
}

    mp ~ normal(0,100);
   
taueps ~ gamma(0.01,0.01);
taureg ~ gamma(0.01,0.01);
Y ~ normal(mean_part, sq_taureg);
for(i in 1:N_subj)
W[i] ~ normal(E * xi[i]',sq_taueps);
}

The program is pretty simple, yet the efficiency of the model is even worse than the winbugs program (even with the parallel computing). I have tried my best to vectorize all the distributions. My questions are that:
(1) is the transformation: mean_part is useful for this kind of model?
(2) May be there is a better way to vectorize the last part: W[i] ~ normal(E * xi[i]', sq_taueps).
(3) Are there suggestions on overall improving the efficiency of the program.

Thank you very much for the advice in advance.

Best regards,
Xiangnan

The program is pretty simple, yet the efficiency of the model is even worse than the winbugs program (even with the parallel computing). I have tried my best to vectorize all the distributions. My questions are that:
(1) is the transformation: mean_part is useful for this kind of model?
Sure, but there are cases where it's not useful. It depends on the data: some parameterizations work better under different data conditions.
(2) May be there is a better way to vectorize the last part: W[i] ~ normal(E * xi[i]', sq_taueps).
No. Not currently.
(3) Are there suggestions on overall improving the efficiency of the program.

Yes. Try:
- work with standard deviation parameters instead of precisions. This reminds me of BUGS / JAGS.
- weakly informative priors. Forget about the conjugacy. Just use something that makes sense. Perhaps normals priors on the standard deviation parameters?

Finally:
- do you have simulated data that matches this model? What happens when you fit that?
If you don't have that, start here.


Daniel

Thank you very much for the advice in advance.

Best regards,
Xiangnan

Dear Daniel,

Thank you very much for the kind help.

I have been using tailor made program in R to conduct Bayesian analysis. I have also tried winbugs and jags. Winbugs is the official software for the class where I am the teaching assistant. I think I am from BUGs. : )

I have simulated data for the model, and although the efficiency is not as I expected, the estimation results are acceptable. 

Since the efficiency is a concern, I have derived all the posterior distributions, and made R codes. It works well and fast. I guess the Stan could be used to deal with this kind of latent variable models, but is still not the best one.

I will try other kinds of priors for the models in stan, yet if I use normal prior for the variance component, it may generates negative values, which contradicts the predefined range of the variance parameters. Anyway, I will try. Thank you very very much for the kind help. I will continue using stan to learn using it wisely. : )

Best regards,
Xiangnan

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] On the efficiency of the mixed effect model
parts:
> On Jul 21, 2015, at 4:06 PM, Xiangnan Feng <fengxia...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Dear Daniel,
>
> Thank you very much for the kind help.
>
> I have been using tailor made program in R to conduct Bayesian analysis. I have also tried winbugs and jags. Winbugs is the official software for the class where I am the teaching assistant. I think I am from BUGs. : )
>
> I have simulated data for the model, and although the efficiency is not as I expected, the estimation results are acceptable.
>
> Since the efficiency is a concern, I have derived all the posterior distributions, and made R codes. It works well and fast. I guess the Stan could be used to deal with this kind of latent variable models, but is still not the best one.

Wha are you measuring for efficiency? Effective samples per second
after multiple chains have converged to low R-hat values?

Are you sure your code is recovering the right values and posterior
uncertainty?

> I will try other kinds of priors for the models in stan, yet if I use normal prior for the variance component, it may generates negative values, which contradicts the predefined range of the variance parameters.

That's not how Stan works. If you declare a parameter like this:

parameters {
real<lower=0> sigma;
...
model {
sigma ~ normal(0, 1);

then it applies a *half*-normal prior to sigma. What would be equivalent to
explicit truncation in BUGS:

sigma ~ dnorm(0, 1) T[0, ]

or whatever symbol BUGS uses for truncation.
> Anyway, I will try. Thank you very very much for the kind help. I will continue using stan to learn using it wisely. : )

> My code on the mixed effect model is as follows:
>
> data {
> int<lower=0> N_subj; // usually large = 1000
> int<lower=0> N_obs; // usually smaller = 200
> int<lower=0> K_x; // can be 30
> real Y[N_subj];
> matrix[N_obs, K_x] E;
> matrix[N_subj, N_obs] W;
> }
>
> parameters {
> real mp;
> vector[K_x] beta;
> matrix[N_subj, K_x] xi;
> real<lower=0> taureg;
> real<lower=0> taueps;
> real<lower=0> ll[K_x];
> }
>
> transformed parameters {
> real<lower = 0> sq_taureg;
> real<lower = 0> sq_taueps;
> vector[N_subj] mean_part;
> sq_taureg <- 1/sqrt(taureg);
> sq_taueps <- 1/sqrt(taueps);
> mean_part <- mp + xi * beta;
> }
>
> model {
>
> for (i in 1:N_subj)
> xi[i] ~ normal(0, ll);

Vectorize using:

to_vector(xi) ~ normal(0, ll);

> for (i in 1:K_x){
> ll[i] ~ inv_gamma(0.01,0.01);
> beta[i] ~ normal(0,100);

These can be vectorized, but we really don't recommend these
attempts at "noninformative" priors for statistical reasons.
The vectorizations would just be

ll ~ inv_gamma(0.01, 0.01);
beta ~ normal(0, 100);

We'd more typically use something like this:

ll ~ cauchy(0, 2)

and this

beta ~ normal(0, 1);

> }
>
> mp ~ normal(0,100);
>
> taueps ~ gamma(0.01,0.01);
> taureg ~ gamma(0.01,0.01);
> Y ~ normal(mean_part, sq_taureg);
> for(i in 1:N_subj)
> W[i] ~ normal(E * xi[i]',sq_taueps);

One way to make this more efficient is to change the declaration of x from

> matrix[N_subj, K_x] xi;


to

vector[K_x] xi[N_subj];

Same thing for the W matrix.

Then the copy is free and you don't have to transpose.

Those gamma(0.01, 0.01) are bad news for all the reasons Andrew Gelman's
written about, both statistically and computationally. See the references
in the manual (regression chapter discussion of priors) or in Bayesian
Data Analysis (Gelman et al.'s book).

For the same reason, normal(0,100) is rarely what you want unless your
parameter mp can take on values in the +/- 100s.

It can also make a big difference to efficiency to standardize
all your predictors.

> }
>
> The program is pretty simple, yet the efficiency of the model is even worse than the winbugs program (even with the parallel computing). I have tried my best to vectorize all the distributions. My questions are that:
> (1) is the transformation: mean_part is useful for this kind of model?

I'm not sure what you mean here. If you don't care about mean_part (what
is often called y_hat in the literature), then you don't need to define
it in transformed parameters because it's going to get saved every iteration,
which is relatively slow in R.

>
> Sure, but there are cases where it's not useful. It depends on the data: some parameterizations work better under different data conditions.

Daniel --- this isn't a different parameterization, just precomputing
the mean vector to vectorize.

> (2) May be there is a better way to vectorize the last part: W[i] ~ normal(E * xi[i]', sq_taueps).
>
> No. Not currently.

Not quite, but there's a slightly more efficient way to write it. See above.

I wouldn't use sq_taueps for 1 / sqrt(taueps) --- it's misleading.
maybe invsqrt_taueps if you like verbose names.

Also, it looks like you're parameterizing on the wrong scale. We use
standard deviation, not variance. So if your parameter tau is precision,
you need

sigma <- 1 / sqrt(tau)

- Bob
